      <title>ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/04/anc-south-africa-local-elections-water-outages-power-cuts</link>
      <description><p>Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts</p><p>The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.</p><p>The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls show it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the <a href="https://results.elections.org.za/dashboards/lge/">last municipal elections</a> in 2021 and 40.2% in <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/article/2024/jun/02/south-africa-election-anc-coalition-talks-ramaphosa">2024’s national elections</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/04/anc-south-africa-local-elections-water-outages-power-cuts">Continue reading...</a></description>

        <media:credit scheme="urn:ebu">Photograph: Themba Hadebe/AP</media:credit>

News from the US, Europe, Asia Pacific, Africa, Middle East, America</description><link>https://www.france24.com/en/</link><lastBuildDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 08:07:02 GMT</lastBuildDate><atom:link href="https://www.france24.com/en/rss" rel="self" type="application/rss+xml"/><item><category></category><title>Midterms: What impact did redistricting in California and Texas have?</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261104-midterms-what-impact-did-redistricting-in-california-and-texas-have</link><description>
Last year, California voters approved a bill to temporarily redraw the state’s congressional map to make certain congressional districts more favourable to the Democrats – itself a response to a Republican-led redistricting push that began in Texas. France 24’s Wassim Cornet in Los Angeles takes a look at what impact these efforts may have had on the midterm results.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/81358b96-d824-11f1-b369-a575454bc579/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261104-082208-082716-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/81358b96-d824-11f1-b369-a575454bc579/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261104-082208-082716-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">85f3ca26-d824-11f1-884c-ffb9ca698650</guid><pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 08:03:10 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>Blue wave 'turning into a tsunami' as Democrats take control of Congress</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261104-blue-wave-turning-into-a-tsunami-as-democrats-take-control-of-congress</link><description>
Democrats seized control of both the Senate and House at the US midterms on November 3, scoring sweeping victories in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations as tens of millions of voters delivered a scathing rebuke to President Donald Trump. Many analysts had predicted a "blue wave" would sweep the elections, but that is now "heading into tsunami territory", says France 24's international affairs editor Kethevane Gorjestani.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/9e16a558-d822-11f1-805e-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261104-080944-081226-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/9e16a558-d822-11f1-805e-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261104-080944-081226-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">a2d1140c-d822-11f1-8cc9-b10be35813e9</guid><pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 07:51:12 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>US midterms: Democrat James Talarico wins Senate race in deep-red Texas</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261104-us-midterms-democrat-james-talarico-wins-senate-race-in-deep-red-texas</link><description>
🇺🇸 Democrat James Talarico said Tuesday that "we defeated Goliath" after winning a US Senate seat over Texas attorney General Ken Paxton.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/4e1b8168-d822-11f1-85b0-1beafce15fea/w:1024/p:16x9/Talarico.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/4e1b8168-d822-11f1-85b0-1beafce15fea/w:1024/p:16x9/Talarico.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">2442e24e-d81a-11f1-a444-67ce9b454317</guid><pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 07:36:28 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>Talarico says 'power belongs to the people' as Democrats win big in Texas</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261104-talarico-says-power-belongs-to-the-people-as-democrats-win-big-in-texas</link><description>
Democrat James Talarico flipped a US Senate seat in Texas on Tuesday, defeating Republican Ken Paxton to pull off the first statewide victory in more than 30 years and sending a jolt through a longtime GOP stronghold that President Donald Trump carried by double digits just two years ago. In another political earthquake for the southern border state, Democrat Gina Hinojosa unseated incumbent Texas Governor Greg Abbott. France 24's correspondent in Texas Andres Espinal has the latest.

<![CDATA[ Latest from Space.com ]]> https://www.space.com/feeds.xml Tue, 03 Nov 2026 22:00:00 +0000 en <![CDATA[ NASA asks industry for ideas about saving Hubble Space Telescope ]]> NASA is reviving discussions to rescue the Hubble Space Telescope, which is operating well but is on track to reenter Earth's atmosphere about six years from now.

The agency issued a request for information (RFI) on Oct. 29 for "in-space servicing" capabilities, which could include boosting Hubble's orbit (which is naturally degrading due to atmospheric drag), or even a mission to "enhance its capabilities" in some way.

Hubble, which launched in April 1990 in partnership with the European Space Agency, was serviced five times by astronauts on space shuttle missions, the most recent being in 2009. The observatory's groundbreaking achievements include helping to show that the expansion of the universe is accelerating — a discovery that won the Nobel Prize — as well as a swath of finds about planets, galaxies, stars and other parts of the universe.

Hubble also regularly teams up with other telescopes for science work, and its observations have led to the publication of at least 23,000 scientific papers, NASA figures suggest. And, despite its age, Hubble remains in high demand. "Astronomers request about seven times as much observing time as is available each year," the agency stated in September.

Hubble is also widely appreciated by the public. People have long enjoyed and celebrated its iconic images, such as the Eagle Nebula's "Pillars of Creation," a gorgeous shot that has been revisited several times over the decades. As such, this is not the first time in recent years that discussions have opened about keeping the famed observatory running for a while longer.

In 2022, for example, billionaire tech entrepreneur Jared Isaacman proposed using SpaceX hardware to mount a Hubble-servicing mission. (Isaacman also purchased and commanded two crewed SpaceX missions to Earth orbit, which flew in September 2021 and September 2024.) NASA declined, however, citing possible risks to the healthy observatory.

But things have changed, apparently. Isaacman, who in December 2025 became NASA administrator, said in an Oct. 30 agency statement that Hubble's science return means the agency should "be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible" — especially if doing so would be a cost savings compared with launching another mission.

In an Oct. 30 post on X, Isaacman added that it's "still worth exploring the options" and noted that NASA had previously considered "a far lower-cost solution" to keep the observatory flying. "That was then. Still worth the effort — Hubble deserves it," he added.

The new RFI also allows for alternative scenarios, however, which could include a "safe, controlled reentry into Earth's atmosphere or orbital disposal at the end of Hubble's mission."

Hubble will naturally enter the atmosphere in 2033 or 2034 due to orbital drag, so any attempt to service it would have to be in 2032, the agency stated.

Earlier this year, NASA worked with Katalyst Space Technologies on a $30 million mission that aimed to boost the orbit of the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, which is also falling back to Earth due to orbital drag.

That long-shot rescue mission — which was developed quickly to race against accelerated solar activity, which ballooned Earth's atmosphere and increased drag — launched successfully this summer. But control issues prevented Katalyst's LINK spacecraft from meeting up with Swift. Swift is expected to reenter Earth's atmosphere tomorrow (Nov. 4) after 22 years of operations — far past its two-year design lifetime.

]]> <![CDATA[ Ancient star collisions could explain mysterious Little Red Dots and 'impossible' black holes ]]> New research suggests that collisions between stars in the early universe were common, which could help explain the rapid growth of supermassive black holes and the existence of strange Little Red Dots seen by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

The team behind this research performed simulations of the early universe and found stellar systems were densely packed, leading to stars frequently slamming into each other. While rapid collisions would have destroyed the stars involved, slower collisions would have led to repeated mergers, creating single over-massive stars, which could collapse and form larger-than-usual black holes at the end of their lives. These could be the seeds of the first supermassive black holes.

Dense stellar environments do still exist in the modern universe at the hearts of galaxies; however, these aren't conducive to the types of collisions that would birth ultra-massive stars. That is because there are already supermassive black holes at the hearts of modern galaxies, and their immense gravitational influence speeds up orbiting stars, meaning collisions that do occur are high-speed and destructive, thus failing to birth overmassive stars.

"Perhaps the strangest outcome of our simulations is that stars can merge repeatedly within the cluster until they form one gigantic star with a mass equal to that of an entire cluster," team member Claire Williams, of the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), said in a statement. "When a star this huge reaches the end of its life, models suggest that it may have no option but to collapse into itself and form a massive black hole."

My, haven't you grown? How did supermassive black holes get so big so fast?

The existence of supermassive black holes before the universe was even 1 billion years old is something that has puzzled astronomers since the JWST started spotting them in 2022.

This is because black holes should need at least 1 billion years to complete the feeding and merger processes that result in a "supermassive" status of possessing millions or billions of times the mass of the sun.

One suggestion put forward by scientists to explain this is that supermassive black holes don't start out from scratch. Instead, they form from black hole seeds called intermediate-mass black holes.

Normally, when a massive star collapses, it births a stellar-mass black hole possessing a mass between 10 and 100 times the mass of the sun. This is considerably smaller than supermassive black holes that dominate the hearts of all modern galaxies with masses millions to billions of times the mass of our star.

Intermediate-mass black holes are thought to sit between these two families of cosmic titans with masses between 100 and 100,000 times that of the sun. The problem is, no single star should have enough mass to collapse and create an intermediate-mass black hole. But that is valid only for the conditions we see in the "modern" 13.8-billion-year-old universe in our immediate cosmic vicinity. Conditions were very different further out into the universe and further back in time.

Indeed, such seeds emerged from these new simulations in environments of dense star clustering, which could solve this mystery by allowing those growth processes to get a head start.

"Dense star clusters provide a natural birthplace for massive black-hole seeds in our model," Williams said. "The same environment that forms the black hole can also provide stars and gas that influence its subsequent growth."

However, this could be a two-for-one deal. The JWST has also been routinely discovering astronomical bodies called Little Red Dots in the early universe. Little Red Dots are curious because they seem to have completely disappeared by the time the cosmos reached 2 billion years old.

Little Red Dots the cosmic elephant in the room

Little Red Dots are extremely compact objects in the early universe that get their moniker from the fact that they look like red dots.

"Little Red Dots are a hot topic in astronomy. You can compare studies of people trying to understand Little Red Dots to the tale of blind people who are trying to describe an elephant by touching it, and each person describes it differently based on what part they’re touching," team member and UCLA researcher Smadar Naoz said. "Our research connects several of those perspectives together and may help us see more of the elephant."

There have been many suggestions about the true nature of these objects, but one theory suggests that they possess a rapidly growing black hole at their hearts.

The team's simulations suggest that Little Red Dots may be dense star clusters that are constantly being rocked by repeated stellar collisions. This results in a very large star, which eventually collapses to become an intermediate-mass black hole.

But if that is the case, why were there no Little Red Dots around to celebrate the 2 billionth birthday of the universe?

Less than 1 billion years after the Big Bang, the universe was devoid of well-ordered spiral galaxies, but was instead filled with dense and chaotic clusters of star birth. As these regions were rocked with frequent star collisions, the conditions were right for ultra-massive stars to form and collapse into intermediate-mass black holes.

However, as the universe cooled and expanded, these sites became the building blocks of far less chaotic galaxies. Thus, if Little Red Dots are chaotic star clusters needed to form intermediate-mass black holes, progress toward an equilibrium state could explain why they suddenly disappeared from the universe. The cosmos just wasn't extreme enough to maintain Little Red Dots anymore.

The team's research was published on Monday (Oct. 26) in the Astrophysical Journal.

]]> <![CDATA[ 'OGame' developers explain how the browser-based sci-fi game has lasted 24 years ahead of the huge Orion update ]]> If you were on the Internet in the early 2000s looking for free browser games to play, OGame was a blooming sci-fi strategy sensation that couldn't be ignored. With online servers providing the structure for a living and evolving universe where players fought, traded, and created empires from scratch, its limited visual presentation was no issue.

Times have changed, but GameForge hasn't gone anywhere. OGame has been ported to mobile devices, and content updates have kept it alive and fresh for much longer than a plethora of installable MMO games.

With the Orion update, which will hit the newly launched universes (servers) on November 6, OGame is introducing conflicts against non-player-character (NPC) enemies, wave-based battles, co-op missions, and completely new systems that can also be disrupted by other players.

The game's endurance and such a major reinvention are stunning achievements, so we asked GameForge's Martin Liedtke (Director, Products of Browser Games) and Enrico Mareth (Senior Project Manager for OGame PC and Mobile) about the many challenges of working on OGame alongside the community for so long, what Orion is bringing to the table, and what's next for this worldwide phenomenon.

Some quotes have been editorialized and lightly trimmed for better flow.

"OGame has an enduring core: You build an interstellar empire, and your decisions matter... Keeping it fresh means adding meaningful choices to that foundation," said Liedtke. "Orion adds missions against automated opponents (PvE) alongside missions open to other players (PvP)... It supports different appetites for risk."

The GameForge veteran noted, however, that it's the community that "supplies another kind of freshness" after the studio releases the new content. "We develop the systems; players create much of the history."

Part of this approach is keeping tabs on how very different kinds of players approach what's available. "Some commanders concentrate on their economy; others enjoy expeditions or carefully coordinated fleet operations... Orion follows that approach; more experienced players can dig into fleet composition, progression, and cooperation. The aim is to offer worthwhile choices."

Liedtke also noted that "OGame's PvP has become a sophisticated contest of information and coordination" over time. Some players like to scout targets and organize combined attacks when enemy fleets are vulnerable. Those battles resolve automatically, but it's the planning that "can be remarkably intricate," especially after so many years of updates.

The PvE in Orion doesn't sacrifice any of those intricacies or density. In fact, it's adding a "more structured layer" that gives players clear objectives. In most cases, they'll have to cooperate to obtain better rewards. "There is a strong case for introducing that kind of cooperative PvE earlier. It gives players another reason to build and use fleets together."

Over two decades later, how people choose to engage with OGame has changed, pushing GameForge to consider supporting new platforms. Today, mobile devices have become essential to free-to-play games' success over time.

Mareth told us their importance "has made touch controls, navigation, and clarity on smaller screens central development considerations," even if thousands of players still remain attached to PC as their main platform. "We're currently working on a design overhaul of the app, combining what we've learned with players' feedback."

Liedtke also said there is more overlap between PC and mobile players than you might imagine.

"The same player might check their empire on a phone and spend a longer session planning in the browser." Liedtke also noted that "Different playstyles also have different needs," adding that activities like mining and trading fit "comfortably" into short mobile sessions, but complex fleet operations benefit from sitting in front of one's PC.

While it's a game of interstellar conflict and sci-fi spaceships, OGame does take a lot of inspiration from real-life science, even if it stretches that science well past its limits. "When ships are destroyed in battle, the debris field can form a moon around a player's planet," explains Liedtke. "The chance (of that happening) is linked to the real lunar cycle: it is higher around a full moon than a new moon."

He noted it's a "playful connection" to astronomy, "rather than a simulation of how real moons form," but the developers thought it was cool to influence the game via things that happen in our own sky.

This possible in-game "event" also led to one of the best examples of player ingenuity in OGame: Moonshots. Liedtke explained that "players organize deliberate battles and exchange sacrificial fleets to help one another obtain those valuable moons. They have turned destruction into a cooperative project. For a designer, the lesson is to examine what players can achieve together, as well as what an individual action rewards."

As the team figured out how to develop "the more imaginative side of science fiction" in OGame's universe, they also decided to explicitly use deuterium for fusion research and as fuel. Star Trek fans will recognize this as the starship fuel of that universe, but it is a real substance: one of two stable isotopes of hydrogen. "Those scientific references give the universe familiar foundations," remarks Liedtke.

In OGame's shared galaxy, Orion is introducing "anomalies" as a central new feature, which Liedtke described as "mission sites you uncover with a new scanner" before it's required to send in ships. "Combat missions ask you to hold position against waves of automated fleets; peaceful missions put your cargo ships to work collecting rewards." The twist is these missions are open to co-op... but also to rival commanders that can attack the objectives marked as PvP. While you can theoretically ignore them, better rewards await for daring commanders.

With PvE bringing all sorts of new design opportunities to the table, Liedtke pointed out the Orion update "gives us a foundation to learn which kinds of missions players find rewarding" as GameForge looks to the strategy MMO's future. "Personally, I would like to explore encounters that make commanders reconsider what to send and how to work together. Discovery becomes more interesting when it changes your plan."

Sounds exciting, though Liedtke quickly added that this isn't an official announcement of future features.

OGame's 25th anniversary is in 2027, and while the team is tight-lipped on what the team has planned, Liedtke noted that "Reaching a quarter of a century in 2027 will be an extraordinary moment for OGame. We owe that longevity to the team's continued work and, above all, to the players who keep building empires, forming alliances, and giving this universe its stories."

OGame is available on PC (via browser and GameForge's own platform) and on mobile devices via the App Store and Google Play. The Orion update arrives on November 6, 2026.

]]> <![CDATA[ Dimorphos in sight: Europe's Hera probe gets its 1st look at battered space rock (photo) ]]> Europe's Hera planetary defense spacecraft is closing in on the binary asteroid system targeted by NASA's DART deflection test, and can now tell the two rocky bodies apart.

Hera is nearing the end of its voyage to the Didymos asteroid system, having launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket in October 2024. The spacecraft snapped the image of Didymos and the smaller Dimorphos on Oct. 18 from a distance of 795 miles (1280 kilometers) from the pair, which are currently about 122 million miles (197 million km) from Earth.

"With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time," Michael Kueppers, Hera project scientist at the European Space Agency (ESA), said in a statement. "Before this acquisition, the spacecraft was still resolving the Didymos system as a single dot. But now, even though Dimorphos is made up of only around one pixel in this initial image, it is clearly well separated from its parent body."

The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) smashed into Dimorphos in September 2022, changing the asteroid's orbit in a pioneering planetary defense demonstration. Hera's job is to survey the damage and refine our understanding of the impact, as well as the asteroids themselves.

Hera performed braking maneuvers earlier in October to slow its approach and put it on course to rendezvous with the binary system. The spacecraft is designed to make follow-up observations of the asteroids using 12 payloads, providing new insights that will prove valuable for planetary defense efforts. The mission also carries a pair of cubesats for a closer look and eventual landing on the 495-foot-wide (151 meters) Dimorphos.

For now, Hera is continuing its approach and preparing for arrival, with a big reveal expected to occur later this month.

"Our views will grow much sharper as Hera comes closer," said ESA's mission manager Ian Carnelli. "We will unveil the first detailed images of Dimorphos — the first object in the solar system to have had its orbit measurably shifted by human action — on 25 November."

]]> <![CDATA[ Hubble Telescope sees cosmic 'cat's tail' that could wrap around Earth and the sun 500 times ]]> Using the Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers have investigated a cosmic cat's tail, finding it likely formed after two Pluto-sized bodies smashed together.

The feature, nicknamed the Cat's Tail, extends out from the debris disk known as Beta Pictoris which is located in a planetary system located 63 light-years away. This tail would put that of the average tabby to shame: It's so long that it could curl around the sun-Earth system about 500 times. That's about as long as 200 trillion house cats.

The major difference between our solar system and the planetary system that hosts the Cat's Tail is the latter's relative youth. While our solar system is around 4.6 billion years old, Beta Pictoris is a cosmic kitten no more than a few million years old. That means it is still host to collisions between planetary bodies similar to the ones that rocked the solar system during its infancy.

The team behind this research gained new insights into the Cat's Tail using 14 years of observations. This allowed them to solve the long-standing mystery of the violent conditions under which it formed.

"The Cat's Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies — think something like Pluto," team leader Arin Avsar of the University of Arizona said in a statement. "Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while."

Cosmic cat tail is also pleasingly fluffy

Comparing Beta Pictoris and our solar system, one thing rapidly becomes apparent: our cosmic neighborhood is relatively well-ordered. The planets orbit the sun with most space rocks neatly delegated into bands: the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and the Kuiper belt out beyond the orbit of Neptune.

However, this is a stark contrast to the solar system's violent and chaotic youth. Back then, the solar system was host to an infant star surrounded by a swirling disk of gas and dust in which collisions between bodies called planetesimals — the building blocks of planets — were commonplace.

Astronomers can't look back to the solar system's infancy, so to learn more about how our cosmic backyard took shape, they study nearby young planetary systems. Systems like Beta Pictoris. That doesn't mean it has been quick to divulge its secrets, though.

"We think the Cat's Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it's made of," Avsar explained. "It consists almost entirely of what we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they're quite black."

This new study revealed that the feline feature is cat-like in more ways than just its shape. It's also pleasingly fluffy, Hubble observations suggest. That's because the grains that compose it are extremely porous.

"How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here no one really understands, and that's part of why we study this feature," Avsar said.

"It's possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that's how they became so porous," team member Kevin Wagner of the U of A said.

The scientists also discovered a hitherto undiscovered feature in the Cat's Tail — a warp that seems to be the result of an interaction between the trail of material and one of the planets in the system, Beta Pictoris b, a gas giant planet 10 times more massive than Jupiter.

"This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force," Avsar said. "It's a testament to how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units [one astronomical unit being the distance between Earth and the sun]."

The team's research was published last month in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

]]> <![CDATA[ The Star Wars Eclipse — Want to see the 2027 total solar eclipse on Tatooine? Head to Tunisia ]]> On Aug. 2, 2027, darkness will fall on Tatooine. 1. Eriguet dunes (Mos Espa)

Location: south of Chott el-Gharsa, Tozeur Governorate, southwest Tunisia

Start of totality and duration: 10:06 a.m. CET; 2 minutes, 9 seconds

On Nov. 3, 1957, a Soviet space dog named Laika became the first animal to orbit Earth. Laika was a 3-year-old stray husky-spitz mix from the streets of Moscow, and she was recruited by the Soviet space program for her small size and calm temperament.

Laika has remained one of space history's most beloved and tragic figures. People around the world have dogs as pets who they love as members of their own families. Though, the team behind that flight was so unsure of how it would go that Ham didn't get his name until after it was found that he'd survived his return.

Reminiscent of Rocky rolling around the lab helping out Dr. Ryland Grace in Project Hail Mary, the Astrobee robot is a helpful assistant for astronauts aboard the space station.

The robots are designed to assist the astronauts onboard with testing new technologies in microgravity and helping mission team members back on Earth to better observe inside the station. The idea of a robot assistant helping out with chores and technology development aboard an orbiting space laboratory sounds positively science fiction.

While Astrobee is certainly not the first robot in space or aboard the space station, its compact shape and ability to fly autonomously gives it a unique quality. It really looks like a companion aboard the space station.

While the robotic space helpers of today might be cute little cubes, the success of the Astrobee program begs the question of how robots in space might continue to evolve. Will astronauts on the moon have robotic companions autonomously exploring and helping out? What will they look like?

The mission will launch a Space Launch System (SLS) rocket with the four Artemis IV astronauts aboard NASA's Orion capsule to high Earth orbit, where they will rendezvous and dock with the Starship lunar lander.

Using Starship's engines, the two spacecraft will burn for the moon, and separate upon their arrival in low lunar orbit. Two astronauts will remain aboard Orion, while the other two will head down to the lunar surface in Starship.

After a little run through the regolith and a celebration of America's triumphant return to the moon, the duo will board Starship again to launch back to lunar orbit and dock with Orion before beginning the trip back to Earth.

Orion will rendezvous with Starship in high Earth orbit — but that's not where the lander will launch initially. Then, and this is where some of the head scratching begins, Starship will undock from the depot and raise its altitude to what NASA has labeled the "final tanking orbit," or FTO.

At some point after the Starship lander departs LEO, SpaceX will launch another round of "(multiple)" tanker ships to fill the depot with even more propellant. It will apparently then send the depot to meet the lander for another refill in FTO, where, as the name suggests, the two will dock for the pair's final fuel transfer.

 <description>Na vytoužený konec rozsáhlých stavebních prací v okolí ulice Sluneční si budou muset obyvatelé severní části Moravské Třebové ještě počkat. Tamní silnice totiž zůstává neprůjezdná.  <description>Dostat se na druhý břeh řeky pomocí vlastní síly v gondole zavěšené pod konstrukcí mostu – tak bude fungovat transbordér, který se začal stavět v okrajové části Plzně Malesicích.  <description>Fotbalisti Mokrého u Českých Budějovic se mohou v brzké době těšit na nové zázemí, šatny i tribunu.    <description>Obsah testů jednotné přijímací zkoušky pro střední školy a víceletá gymnázia se změní. Pokud muže spatříte, v žádném případě se ho nesnažte sami zadržet a ihned volejte tísňovou linku 158.</description></item><item><title>Geopark Český ráj přijde o značku UNESCO, nevyřešil problém s prodejem kamenů</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904834-geopark-cesky-raj-prijde-o-znacku-unesco-nevyresil-problem-s-prodejem.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904834-geopark-cesky-raj-prijde-o-znacku-unesco-nevyresil-problem-s-prodejem.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 06:30:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Geopark Český ráj se sídlem v Turnově přijde na konci letošního roku o prestižní značku UNESCO, kterou má od roku 2015. Geopark ji nepřesvědčil, že vyřešil problém s prodejem drahých kamenů nejasného původu.</description></item><item><title>KOMENTÁŘ: Investiční návyky Čechů nemění jen inflace. Velký vliv mají i generační rozdíly</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/blogy-a-komentare/904643-komentar-investicni-navyky-cechu-nemeni-jen-inflace-velky-vliv-maji-i-generacni-rozdily.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/blogy-a-komentare/904643-komentar-investicni-navyky-cechu-nemeni-jen-inflace-velky-vliv-maji-i-generacni-rozdily.html</guid><pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 20:35:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Jan Dragon</dc:creator><category>Blogy a komentáře</category><description>Ekonomické otřesy posledních let, divoká inflace a skokový růst úrokových sazeb, nám všem daly tvrdou lekci. Ukázaly, že nechat úspory ležet na běžném účtu znamená sledovat, jak ztrácejí hodnotu. Čechy to donutilo přemýšlet jinak a celkový fondový kapitál u nás už přesáhl 2,33 bilionu korun.</description></item><item><title>Protest v Liberci: Stovky lidí bránily před radnicí nezávislost ČT a ČRo</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904828-protest-v-liberci-stovky-lidi-branily-pred-radnici-nezavislost-ct-a-cro.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904828-protest-v-liberci-stovky-lidi-branily-pred-radnici-nezavislost-ct-a-cro.html</guid><pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 19:37:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Na náměstí Dr. E. Beneše se 3. listopadu v 16:36 sešly stovky lidí - od studentů přes seniory, herce i zástupce univerzity. Před libereckou radnicí vyjádřili rozhodnou podporu stávkujícím zaměstnancům České televize a Českého rozhlasu v jejich boji za zachování svobodných a nezávislých médií.</description></item><item><title>Liberec jede na cheeseburgerech. Rekordní objednávka McDonald's přesáhla tři tisíce korun</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904652-liberec-jede-na-cheeseburgerech-rekordni-objednavka-mcdonald-s-presahla-tri-tisice-korun.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904652-liberec-jede-na-cheeseburgerech-rekordni-objednavka-mcdonald-s-presahla-tri-tisice-korun.html</guid><pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:57:00 +0100</pubDate><category>Společnost</category><description>Od dubna 2024 doručili kurýři Bolt Food z libereckých restaurací McDonald's přes 9 400 objednávek téměř čtyřem tisícům zákazníků. Nejprodávanější položkou je (ne)obyčejný cheeseburger a nejvíc objednávek padá v pátek a v sobotu večer.</description></item><item><title>Lov na divoká prasata v Jablonci: Město ve čtvrtek uzavře okolí Srnčího dolu</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904759-lov-na-divoka-prasata-v-jablonci-mesto-ve-ctvrtek-uzavre-okoli-srnciho-dolu.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904759-lov-na-divoka-prasata-v-jablonci-mesto-ve-ctvrtek-uzavre-okoli-srnciho-dolu.html</guid><pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:00:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Ve čtvrtek 5. listopadu od 8 do 13 hodin proběhne v okolí Srnčího dolu v Jablonci nad Nisou lov černé zvěře. Cílem myslivců je zregulovat přemnožená divoká prasata, která v posledních týdnech poškozují sportovní areál. Město žádá obyvatele, aby v této době omezili pohyb ve vyznačené oblasti.</description></item><item><title>Opilý tatínek přišel do muzea s holčičkami. Na chodbě zvracel</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/krimi/904755-opily-tatinek-prisel-do-muzea-s-holcickami-na-chodbe-zvracel.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/krimi/904755-opily-tatinek-prisel-do-muzea-s-holcickami-na-chodbe-zvracel.html</guid><pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 14:45:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Luboš Vrabec</dc:creator><category>Krimi</category><description>Tak tenhle nedělní program se tatínkovi se dvěma malými dcerkami nevyvedl. Vyrazil s nimi do Státního muzea skla a bižuterie v Jablonci, jenže nebyl úplně ve formě a na chodbě této instituce se dokonce pozvracel. Zaměstnankyně tak na místo zavolala strážníky.</description></item><item><title>Na Frýdlantsku začnou práce na prvním z projektů financovaných z Fondu Turów</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904626-na-frydlantsku-zacnou-prace-na-prvnim-z-projektu-financovanych-z-fondu.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904626-na-frydlantsku-zacnou-prace-na-prvnim-z-projektu-financovanych-z-fondu.html</guid><pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 13:00:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Ve Frýdlantském výběžku začne stavba desetikilometrového vodovodního přivaděče z Dětřichova do Frýdlantu na Liberecku za zhruba 103 milionů korun. Je to první ze čtyř projektů financovaných z Fondu Turów.</description></item><item><title>Kauza dopravního podniku. Bývalý ředitel Wejnar ani podnikatel Vařil u soudu nevypovídali</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/krimi/904756-soud-v-liberci-se-zacal-zabyvat-korupcni-kauzou-mistniho-dopravniho-podniku.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/krimi/904756-soud-v-liberci-se-zacal-zabyvat-korupcni-kauzou-mistniho-dopravniho-podniku.html</guid><pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 11:52:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Krimi</category><description>V Liberci v pondělí začal soud v korupční kauze kolem místního dopravního podniku. Obžalovaných je sedm lidí a 12 firem, jednu další obžalovanou firmu soud vyloučil do samostatného projednání.</description></item><item><title>McDonald's otevírá registrace do 28. ročníku fotbalového turnaje pro školy</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904696-mcdonald-s-otevira-registrace-do-28-rocniku-fotbaloveho-turnaje-pro-skoly.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904696-mcdonald-s-otevira-registrace-do-28-rocniku-fotbaloveho-turnaje-pro-skoly.html</guid><pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 10:32:00 +0100</pubDate><category>Společnost</category><description>Školní hřiště se znovu chystají zaplnit dresy, kopačkami a smíchem kamarádů z lavice. Od 1. října startují registrace do 28. ročníku McDonald's Cupu, největšího fotbalového turnaje pro žáky a žákyně základních škol v Česku, který každý rok přivede na hřiště desítky tisíc dětí.</description></item></channel></rss>

]]> Mandava Jazz / Mandau Jazz 2026 – Iva Bittová & Duo Jedlinský–Fischer https://www.vybezek.eu/296291-mandava-jazz-mandau-jazz-2026-iva-bittova-duo-jedlinsky-fischer/ Thu, 29 Oct 2026 18:16:24 +0000 https://www.vybezek.eu/?p=296291 Další večer u Kocoura – Mezinárodní hudební festival Mandava Jazz 2026 tentokrát ve středu 28. října 2026, opět ve varnsdorfském pivovaru Kocour, dorazila Iva Bittová a duo Jedlinský & Fischer.

Stejně jako nedávného Dana Bártu i Ivu Bittovou jsme už zažili několikrát (2011 na Vlčí hoře nebo 2017 v divadle). Vždy jako personu velmi osobitou, která si s nástrojem, hlasem a jazykem (nebo spíš jazyky, chvílemi to vypadalo na hudební esperanto-svahilštinu), dělá co chce. A vždy bravurně. Ačkoli ona sama je většinou tahákem na plakátech a v upoutávkách, sama sebe neupřednostňuje a dává spoustu prostoru všem, se kterými v tu kterou chvíli spolupracuje.

Iva Bittová – zpěv, housle; Jakub Jedlinský – akordeon, zpěv; Pavel Fischer – housle, zpěv

Inu, někdo je Fotograf a umí (snad) zachytit neuchopitelnou atmosféru, vyjádřit obrazem zážitek z hudby. Já mezi takové nepatřím, nejsem fotograf. Jsem jen přítomen.
